doc.title: Howard Alden interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997

title: Saturation of recordings and CD length
summary: He agrees the market is oversaturated as CDs grew from 78 sides to 60-plus minutes.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Do you feel the market is oversaturated with any of that? I mean there’s so much out there.
You mean in terms of recordings?

I guess. I’ve noticed usually at the jazz parties they’ll have the tables set up with the CDs. And there’s so much. And I feel like gee I wish I could buy one of each, because I’m sure all these guys deserve to have their CDs bought.

I think it could be actually. I mean again, it’s so — there’s been so much of it and I mean and just on one CD. When you go to make a record — now — of course they started out like 78s, making two good sides you know, or maybe four sides in a day. Then it became LPs and people were making 30 or 40 minutes of music. And now everybody’s trying to make at least 60 minutes of music and maybe more, so the consumer doesn’t feel like they’re being gypped. And so you’re trying to fit all this stuff on. It’s hard, sometimes you just want to make a more concise statement sometimes. But yeah it is pretty saturated to tell you the truth, and you’ve got to — I mean if someone who is relatively new to jazz goes to a record store, they really have to either be guided or know what they’re looking for, and then of course it’s just impossible to keep up with all the new stuff that’s coming out. There’s so many — there’s a lot of great artists out and they’re putting out so much, but you don’t know where to start. So that’s just the way it is I guess.
